title: Family Coresidence, Parent–Child Interaction, and Deviant Behavior Among Rural Chinese Adolescents
abstract: Family coresidence can structure adolescents’ access to parental guidance, but evidence often separates living arrangements from parenting processes. We analyzed 3612 rural-hukou adolescents from 110 schools in the China Education Panel Survey. Deviant behavior was measured as a five-item summed score (5–25). Primary ordinary least squares models used the untransformed score, school-clustered inference, and a core set of stable or plausibly pre-exposure covariates; expanded-control, log-outcome, multiple-imputation, item-level, and instrumental-variable models served as sensitivity analyses. Exploratory coefficient-product models assessed parental supervision and parent–child communication as parallel indirect associations. In the primary binary model, not living with both parents was associated with a 0.312-point higher score (95% CI [0.114, 0.510]). In the four-category model, the clearest multiplicity-adjusted association concerned adolescents living with neither parent (b = 0.388, 95% CI [0.148, 0.628]); estimates for the two one-parent groups were less precise. Multiple imputation supported the binary and neither-parent patterns. School-level instrumental-variable estimates were positive but imprecise and were interpreted as triangulation rather than causal identification. Lower supervision and less frequent communication formed statistically detectable indirect associations, although the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal mediation. Item-level analyses indicated that the composite association was not uniform across behaviors. The findings support a structural–process account while defining clear limits on causal and measurement interpretation.
